notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa054a.opp-l: Many scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Ductus maris' read as 'Fluctus maris'; 'Ignosce' read as 'Agnosce'; 'miserunt' as 'amiserunt'; 'Aunno' as 'Anano'; 'Criolinosam' as 'Criminosam'; 'norum' as 'florum'). In ch. II the clause about David lacks a verb in the text ('David t ... excludere'); read as 'qui solebas ... excludere'. Ch. III opening ('Quid tantum ... Romanus suis armis, quantum populus tuus malorum invexit?') is awkwardly transmitted; rendered by sense. The Psalm cited is Vulgate Ps. 78 (Hebrew 79).

Line 9: 'et spiritus divini soluta evanuerunt' is elliptical; '[places]' supplied from 'sancta' above. Line 10: the figure 'vicies centena, aut septingenta millia' looks corrupt; Josephus gives 2,700,000 (probably 'vicies septies centena millia'). 'gynaecici' is unclear, perhaps a corruption of a Greek term for gonorrhoea sufferers. Line 13: 'a praedicando' read as 'a precando' (by praying). Line 14: 'dccies' read as 'undecies' (1,100,000, as in Josephus, matching '110 myriads'). 'utilitas' read as 'vilitas' (cheapness). 'Rex Justus' is Melchizedek. 'sub corona' means sold as slaves.

In XIII the prayer 'supplicaturus pro papula' read as pro populo. In XIV 'cumulandæ gentis' is translated 'exalted'; the sense is uncertain. 'Muricula' in XVI is read as rusticus ('a rustic man'). 'Nox a quatuor bentis' is read as vox a quatuor ventis. 'Luctibus' near the end of XVI is read as noctibus.

Ch. XVIII: 'Nullus venire locus' read as 'nullus veniae locus' (no room for pardon); 'intestus' read as 'infestus'. Ch. XIX: 'quique Romanorum arma viderunt' must mean the Caesarean Jews saw no Roman arms; a negative seems to have dropped out, supplied in brackets. 'quod prohibuerunt ipsi Sen in gentibus' is corrupt; rendered by sense. The Alexandria passage is in reported speech in the Latin. Ch. XX: 'non quod defecerit clades, sed quod jam nulla requies' is obscure; rendered literally. Ch. XXII: 'ex Patre' read as 'ex parte' (in part). 'Matt. iv, 24' in the text should be Matt. 15:24. Ch. XXIII: 'adversionis' probably for 'eversionis' (overthrow); the Romans reference 'IX, 2' corrected to 9:27.

nodes.text: A RECAPITULATION OF THE HISTORY OF THE DESTRUCTION OF THE CITY OF JERUSALEM, THAT IS, A REPETITION of almost everything that has been said in the preceding books.
CHAPTER ONE.

In the forty-second year after the Lord's passion, and the first of Vespasian's reign, Judaea was being torn apart by fierce wars and by internal uprisings. Their city of Jerusalem itself was also suffering from civil fighting. There was no break, no rest, no truce; they fought at every moment. Many fell, countless people had their throats cut. Blood defiled everything and filled even the thresholds of the temple. Corpses fell everywhere: some were struck by arrows, others by missiles. No place was free of danger; there was no hope of change, no chance of flight: everything was grim and full of horror and full of savagery: everywhere mourning, everywhere fear: the cries of women, the wailing of old men, the groans of the dying, the despair of the living, so that you would call those who remained wretched, and those who died blessed. How have you been betrayed by your own peoples, among whom you once seemed blessed? How have you been overcome by your own arms, and your hands turned against you, you who used to conquer without arms and strike the enemy without any battle, when angels fought for you, and the waves of the sea, the gaping of the earth and the crashing of the heavens served as soldiers for you?
CHAPTER II.

Rise up now, Moses, and see your nation and the inheritance of the people entrusted to you perishing by its own hands: look at that people of God, for whom the sea lay open as a path when it walked, for whom heaven supplied food when it hungered, now shut in without a sea, besieged without a Pharaoh, starving without any barrenness of the land. Rise up, Aaron, you who once, when because of an offence against God death was devouring a great many of the people, stood between the living and the dead, and death stopped, and the plague halted at the barrier of your body and could not pass on to infect the living. You too, rouse yourself, Joshua son of Nun, who levelled the impregnable walls of Jericho while the trumpets sounded; and see that the very people to whom you subjected foreigners is now itself subjected and crushed. Rouse yourself, David, [who used] to drive out a raging spirit by the sweetness of the lyre alone, and see how fury held sway, and has washed all the sweetness of your psalms out of the minds of the lost, and how each one of the leaders brings the whole people to death in order to wring from it the liberty for which you offered yourself to death. Rouse yourself, Elisha, who led the enemy into Samaria and made him a friend. Through you the rumble of chariots resounded in the camp of Syria, and the sound of horsemen and of a mighty host: the enemy fled, the Jew escaped the siege. Where now are those merits, and where now are those works of the saints? Nor is it surprising if those who rejected the judgement of the prophets have lost the works of the prophets. That is why, Judaea, arms are turned against you, and your prayers do you no good, because your faith does no work: that is why your own people has become your enemy, because your faithlessness has been turned against you. What remedy is sought, where the author of the remedy is not won over? What did you think would happen, when you extinguished your life with your own hands, when with your own voices you destroyed your advocate, except that you would also lay hands on yourself? You have what you asked for. You took from yourself the guardian of peace, you demanded that the judge of your life be killed, and that Barabbas be granted to you, who had been thrown into prison for an uprising made in the city and for murder (Luke 23:19): that is why salvation has left you, peace has gone, quiet has ceased: uprising has been given you, destruction has been given you. Recognise that today Barabbas lives for you, and Jesus is dead. That is why uprising reigns in you and peace is buried, so that you perish more cruelly at the hands of your own, and before you could perish at the hands of strangers.
CHAPTER III.

Wretched city, what evil did the Roman bring upon you with his arms so great as your own people brought? Your own people saw to it that you fought the Romans: the Romans wanted peace, you declared war. What reason was there to provoke those stronger [than you]? Granted, it may be hard that a gentile entered the temple against the sacred law: but it was no longer the temple of God. You were not the city of God, nor could you be, since you were a tomb of the dead: especially of your own, whom you yourself had killed, not whom you had lost to the enemy. For how could you be the dwelling of life, you who were the abode of death, the lodging-house of crimes, the den of robbers? Ananus and John, chief priests, lay in you unburied; and those men, lately clothed in priestly robes, who had been held in reverence even by foreigners, lay disfigured. Their corpses became food for birds and prey for dogs, their limbs torn and scattered through the whole city, so that the very image of the old sanctity seemed to lament so great an insult to the sacred name and the disfigurement of an office once splendid. But you yourself made the beginning of this indignity, you who killed the prophets in your very bosom, who stoned the saints of the Lord. Before the temple Zechariah lay lifeless, lay unburied: therefore your blood washes him. And what was the cause of Ananus' death, except that he rebuked your people because it would not rise up in defence of the temple, because he demanded back the lost liberty, the abandoned courage, the trampled remnants of the ancient rites, the defiled altars; he declared that the people should be abandoned, defiled as it was by the use of senseless idols and now feeling nothing, like statues? For even dumb animals usually pay back in revenge, feel an injury, are spurred by the goad, avoid blows. So whoever is neither roused nor knows how to avoid what harms him is like things without feeling.
CHAPTER IV.

And truly, where is your liberty, out of zeal for which you once thought you should yield not to the Egyptians, not to the Philistines, not to the Assyrians, nor later to the Medes? Where is that faith of the Maccabees, which once, in a few men, routed the Babylonians, put the Persians to flight, struck down Demetrius; and finally, in little children and women, overcame the arms, sword and fires of Antiochus, and preferred to die for the observance of the ancestral [law] rather than obey royal commands? Where is that devotion of the fathers, the most beautiful of all sufferings, by which they offered themselves to death not more for their children or wives than for the temple of God? Formerly even the priestly rod, cut from a wild root, blossomed: now faith withers, piety is buried, and all emulation of virtue has gone. Nor is it surprising if a people that has departed from God and follows the wicked spirit of contradiction is divided against itself. For how could it keep its own peace, when it rejected the peace of God? The peace of God is Christ, who made both one (Ephesians 2:14). Rightly, then, out of one people many have become enemies to one another, because they would not follow Jesus who unites what is divided, but followed the spirit of fury that divides what is joined.
CHAPTER V.

So you were paying, Jerusalem, the wages of your faithlessness, when with your own hands you destroyed your own defences, when with your own blades you pierced your own vitals, so that the enemy took pity, so that he spared and you raged. For they saw that God was fighting against you and taking the Romans' part, so that you brought voluntary ruin upon yourself: therefore the Romans preferred to be spectators rather than slayers, lest, while your own vitals raged against one another, they should be thought to lay hands on them out of contagion rather than courage. To the tortures of this unspeakable slaughter was added an impious savagery of cruelty, that they denied burial to all who had been killed either in the temple or about the streets of the city: nor did anyone have time to bury, while they were occupied in wars with each other, and concern with striking rather than burying held everyone. Thus by a kind of fury the duties of piety had died, the services of impiety grew fiercer; and nothing had perished more in such great calamities than mercy, which alone usually relieves miseries and consoles hardships. For those who had lost their own did not dare to bury them out of fear, since heavy terror pressed upon them from the leaders of the opposing faction: and those who had killed kept watch on others, lest anyone snatch [the bodies] away for burial. So everyone had to fear that they would bring on themselves what they wished to give another; or, what is worse, that they themselves would not obtain the use of a tomb which they had prepared.
CHAPTER VI.

In the temple, then, instead of sweet-smelling ointments, instead of fragrant censers, instead of the scents of various flowers, there was the heavy stench of unburied corpses, which the rain had dissolved, which flame had scorched, which the sun had heated. All the limbs of the slain citizens reeked with a dreadful smell. On one side the rot of decomposing entrails, on the other the reek of the burned filled all the senses and mouths of the living, so that not long after they themselves were consumed by a more grievous sickness, and the survivors groaned that they perished by a harsher penalty, and had been preserved only to see the laws of nature dissolved along with their country, right denied to the living, peace to citizens, burial to the dead, human and divine things alike stained and polluted, everything thrown together; mercy treated as a crime, cruelty held in place of religion, a fortress in the temple, war on the threshold, death on the altars; to see with their eyes things which they had not believed would happen when the prophets foretold them. For David had said of these things: They have polluted your holy temple, they have set the mortal remains of your servants as food for the birds of heaven: they have poured out their blood like water round about Jerusalem, and there was none to bury them (Psalm 78:1-3). For at that time, all at once, the gentines came into the inheritance of God to carry off everything, and the temple was polluted by the deaths of its own, and the corpses of the slain lay unburied as food for birds and for the greed of beasts, blood was shed so that it pooled in the temple, and there was no one to bury, because fury passed from the living onto the dead, and from the dead onto those who were still alive. Someone wished to bury a dead man; he himself was killed. And he who had killed the dead man transferred his anger to the burier, to deny him burial: in turn, the one who had killed the burier killed him, and exercised greater cruelty upon the dead, so that he stripped one who now owed nothing to hatred, and felt no punishment, of the last debt of nature.
CHAPTER VII.

What else could befall those who did not accept the divine oracles? They mocked the announcements of the prophets; they trampled on all that was right, and they themselves hastened what was to come so that it came to pass. For there was an old and frequent saying that Jerusalem would perish and its holy places be burned when the uprising of war attacked the law and the hands of its own people defiled the temple of God. Yet they did not understand even this. For how often was the house of God destroyed! how often an uprising! how often war! And never did that city perish, except when with the hands of its own people they crucified the Lord, the true Temple of God. For which reason they also hear this: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). For what else was it but sacrilege, when they stretched out impious hands against the author of salvation, when they stoned him, when they beat him, when they seized him, when they killed him? Then truly the divine fire consumed their holy places. For after it was burned by the Babylonians, it was restored. Afterwards, destroyed by Pompey, it was rebuilt again. But it was utterly burned when Jesus came, and the [places] of the divine spirit were dissolved and vanished. It was fitting for us, with a fuller lament, to lead the way at a kind of funeral of the ancestral solemnity, and as it were to follow certain obsequies, and to discharge them according to the institutions of our forebears.
CHAPTER VIII.

But let us come to the culmination of the overthrow of Jerusalem and to the casting down of the Jews. Rightly indeed were they to be cast down and held cheap, who had bought from a disciple, at the price of thirty denarii, Jesus, dearer than all prices: not to have him as Lord, but to take him from the land of the living as a wicked man. Therefore justly, cheaper than chaff, they were winnowed from their inheritance into every land by the gentiles, whom they had feared lest they should take away their place and nation. And those who had bought Jesus for thirty denarii to destroy him, justly afterwards saw thirty heads of their own people sold for one denarius, to be mocked. Since, then, almost all the Jews consented with one mind to the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, as vengeance hung over them almost all, gathered from every region for the feast of Unleavened Bread, were surrounded by sudden war: so that first a pestilent plague arose among them from the narrowness of the place, and then, more swiftly, famine. That the city could hold so great a multitude of people was certain from those who had been under Cestius. For when the men of the city were then counted by Florus, who wished to show Nero, who despised the nation, [its size], he had asked the high priests to count the multitude if they could in any way. They, when the feast day called Pascha was at hand, on which they slaughter victims from the ninth hour to the eleventh, and these are made by companies, as it were, of no fewer than ten men each, for it is not permitted to feast alone, and many gather from neighbours: they counted two hundred and fifty-six thousand five hundred victims. Reckoning ten feasters to each, this makes two million, or seven hundred thousand, all holy and pure. For neither lepers nor those with skin blemishes, nor those with a flow of seed, whom they call *gynaecici*, nor women polluted by menstrual blood, nor others who were unclean, were permitted to share in the sacrifices; nor even foreigners, except those who had come for the sake of religion.
CHAPTER IX.

This great multitude was gathered from outside. Then, however, the whole nation was shut in by fate as if into a prison, and the city, stuffed with people, was besieged by war. And so the number of the slain, whom the Romans partly killed openly and partly captured, surpasses every plague, whether human or sent from heaven. For searching the sewers and digging up the tombs, they killed whomever they came upon. More than two thousand were found there, of whom some killed themselves by their own hand, but more by wounds given to one another, when famine had seized the others. For they were paying the penalty of their crimes, who after they crucified Jesus, the arbiter of divine things, afterwards also persecuted his disciples: yet many of the Jews and very many of the gentiles believed in him, being drawn by his moral precepts and by works flowing beyond human possibility; and not even his death put an end to their faith or gratitude: rather it even increased their devotion. They also laid parricidal hands [on him], and led the author of life to Pilate to be killed, and began to press the reluctant judge hard: in which, however, Pilate is not excused, but the madness of the Jews is heaped higher: because neither ought he to have condemned one whom he had found in no way guilty, nor ought they to have doubled sacrilege with parricide, so that he who had offered himself to redeem and heal them should be condemned by them. For although the same Pilate washed his hands, saying: I am clean of the blood of this just man, see to it yourselves (Matthew 27:24): yet he stands no less guilty, who, recognising the glory of the Lord's resurrection, was eager, though unwilling, to proclaim it, but in his faithlessness scorned to believe it, as his own letter, sent to Caesar in this manner, testifies.
CHAPTER X.

Pontius Pilate to Claudius, greetings. It recently happened, and I myself have verified it, that the Jews through envy have punished themselves and their descendants with a cruel condemnation. For when their fathers had a promise that their God would send them from heaven his Holy One, who would rightly be called their King, and he had promised to send him to earth through a Virgin: when, then, the God of the Hebrews had sent him into Judaea while I was governor, and they had seen that he gave light to the blind, cleansed lepers, healed paralytics, drove demons out of people, even raised the dead, commanded the winds, walked with dry feet upon the waves of the sea, and did many other things, and all the people of the Jews said that he was the Son of God, the chief men of the Jews felt envy against him, and seized him and handed him over to me, and told me one lie after another about him, asserting that he was a sorcerer and acted against their law. I believed it was so, and having had him scourged I handed him over to their will. They crucified him, and when he was buried, they set a guard. But while my soldiers were guarding him, he rose on the third day: and the wickedness of the Jews blazed up so far that they gave money to the guards and said: Say that his disciples stole his body (Matthew 28:13). But though they had taken the money, they could not keep silent about what had happened. For they testified that they had seen him risen, and that they had taken money from the Jews.
CHAPTER XI.

We have entered on these things so that no one may lie otherwise, and think that the lies of the Jews are to be believed. Of him the faithless themselves testify, as Josephus, the writer of histories, says that there was at that time a wise man (if indeed, he says, it is right to call him a man), a worker of wonderful deeds, who appeared to his disciples alive after three days of his death, according to the writings of the prophets, who prophesied both these and countless other things about him full of miracles: from whom the congregation of Christians began, and it has penetrated every race of men; nor has any nation of the Roman world remained which was left without a share in his worship. If the Jews do not believe us, let them at least believe their own: Josephus said this, whom they themselves think the greatest. And yet, in that he spoke the truth for the sake of historical faithfulness, because he thought it wrong to deceive, and did not believe because of hardness of heart and the bent of faithlessness: still he does not prejudice the truth because he did not believe, but rather added to the testimony, because, though unbelieving and unwilling, he did not deny it. In this the eternal power of Christ Jesus shone forth, that even the leaders of the synagogue confessed him as God, whom they had seized for death. And truly, speaking as God without respect of persons or any fear of death, he also foretold the coming destruction of the temple; yet it was not the injury to the temple that stirred them. But because he rebuked them for their crimes and sacrileges, from this their anger blazed up, so that they killed him, whose like no ages had had. For while others earned by praying the power to do what they did, he had it in his power to obtain all that he wished to be done.
CHAPTER XII.

So on the eighth day of the month of September the city was burned: those slain over the whole time numbered eleven hundred thousand, one hundred and ten myriads, as most assert: all of them Jews, yet not all of the same region or place, for they had gathered from everywhere at the time of the Passover solemnity: ninety-seven thousand captives were led away. Indeed, because of the great multitude of captives, there was such cheapness that thirty were sold by the Romans as slaves for a single coin. When the siege was finished, then, Caesar Titus ordered the city and the temple to be overturned from their foundations, so that the word of the Lord Jesus might be fulfilled, who proclaimed: Amen I say to you, there shall not be left stone upon stone that shall not be destroyed (Matthew 24:2): such was the end of the siege of Jerusalem. This same city of Jerusalem a certain powerful man of the Canaanites founded, who in his native tongue was called the Just King; he first named it Solyma, and afterwards added the temple: from which the city was called Hierosolyma. From the beginning it had its own inhabitants from the race of the Canaanites. David, the first Hebrew man, drove out the Canaanites and settled his own people, and made himself a royal house in it. He wished also to found a temple for God, but, forbidden by an oracle, he left Solomon as heir to build the temple which he himself had vowed. So Solomon founded the temple. The other kings too added a great deal to the adornment of the city; envy arose from its magnificence.
CHAPTER XIII.

Among all the works, however, the temple excelled, with its most ample workmanship and gleaming marble, [and] a precious and very great curtain, woven of scarlet and hyacinth and fine linen, with purple: not an idle material of such great variety, but one whose kinds signified the mystery of the things they declare, because it was the temple of him who, as creator of the elements, ruled over sky and air, earth and sea, and alone directed and governed all things. For by scarlet the fiery sky is figured, by hyacinth the air, by fine linen the earth, by purple the sea, since purple is dyed with sea-shellfish: so that you gather two from colour and two from origin. Further, the chief of the priests was accustomed to express these four in his vestment when there was the greatest celebration of the feast days, as if he were putting on the whole world, about to make supplication for the people, in the figure of him who was to come as chief of the priests, Jesus, to take away the sin of the world. The chief of the priests covered his thighs with an inner covering of linen, because above all else in a priest faith of mind is sought and chastity of body, which ought to gird up the intemperance of the flesh. There were two sacred tabernacles, one inner, the other outer: into this the priests always entered; into that inner one, which was called holy, the chief of the priests entered once, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the ignorance and offence of the people. By this the Holy Spirit signified that Jesus would come, who alone would truly enter into the inner recesses of the divine mysteries and the ark of the heavenly substance, who alone would know all things; and who would also reconcile the Father to the whole world by his blood, so that he might have mercy on things of heaven and of earth. And indeed, after he came, he made peace through the blood of his cross for all things that are in heaven or on earth (Colossians 1:20).
CHAPTER XIV.

Within was the altar of incense, within the table, within the lamp. The altar of incense, because priestly prayer above all is directed to God the Father just as incense is (Psalm 140:2). The table, because on it is the passion of Christ and the mysteries of the sacraments. Hence David says: You have prepared a table in my sight (Psalm 22:5), whose twelve loaves, as it were, are the twelve Apostles, witnesses of his passion and resurrection. The lamp, which is placed under the lampstand, was formerly under the bushel, that is, the measure of the law: now it is in the fullness of grace, pouring out abundant light from its seven lamps, because the Holy Spirit illuminates the temple of God with the powers of the seven greatest graces. The knowledge of the Trinity, therefore, was in the inner parts of the temple, which were called the Holy of Holies, where once the rod of Aaron, laid up, blossomed: because priestly grace in Christ would work more fully after the death by which he redeemed the world. The Jews, then, had they been willing to believe, had evident signs of the imminent destruction, by which they were warned as if by clear voices that their end was approaching. For for almost a year a comet blazed above the temple itself, in the likeness of a hanging sword, announcing also by sword and fire the coming devastation of the nation and kingdom and of the city itself. For what did the likeness of a sword announce but war, what did fire announce but burning? It was seen, moreover, before the people separated themselves from the Romans. And in the very days of the Pascha, on the eighth day of the eleventh month, every night at about the ninth hour, the temple and its altar shone with such light as if it were day, lasting each day for about half an hour: which the common people interpreted as appearing to be a sign that the nation would be exalted; and by this they were driven on, as though the time had come to recover their liberty. The more prudent, on the contrary, held that this kind of star usually announces war.
CHAPTER XV.

Lest anyone should think that we are speaking of things foreign to our worship and discipline: first, we are not asserting what seems [true] to us, but what happened, and what opinions there were at that time, what the prudent thought and what the imprudent; nor, when something is said about the sect of the Jews, should it seem written by us as though we had set it out as being in the truth of their worship, and not as sent ahead in shadow and figure, so that we might follow more perfect things. For about signs in the stars we are taught even in the Gospel, that there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars (Luke 21:25). They also asserted that a heifer, when she stood at the altar to be sacrificed in the midst of the temple, gave birth to a lamb, during the very celebrations of the rites we mentioned above. Also that the inner eastern gate, heavy with solid bronze, which used to be shut at evening by the labour of twenty men, with iron bars fastened, for several nights opened of its own accord, and was afterwards shut by the guards only with difficulty. This too many thought a sign of good things to come, as though the gate were opened for them to enter: but the wiser said that the guard of the temple appeared to be loosed, so that whatever was inside might be plundered by the enemy, the inner worship would depart and be emptied by devastation, and the celebration of sacrifices would be destroyed; and that this was clearly signified even before they crucified Christ Jesus, the reading [of Scripture] teaches. After many days, too, a certain figure of inestimable size appeared, which very many beheld (as the books of the Jews have shown), and before sunset there were suddenly seen in the clouds chariots and armed battle lines, by which the cities of all Judaea and its region were overrun. And at the very feast of Pentecost, the priests entering the inner parts of the temple at night to celebrate the customary sacrifices reported that first they felt a certain movement and a sound was given; afterwards also that they heard a sudden voice cry out: Let us pass hence.
CHAPTER XVI.

Also Jesus, son of Ananias, a rustic man, four years before the Jewish people undertook the war, when the city was in the greatest peace and plenty, and the solemn sacrifices of the Feast of Tabernacles were being celebrated, went up into the temple and began to cry out: A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem, against the temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against the whole people. This he shouted night and day. The leading men of the place, disturbed, seized him, shuddering at the terrible portent of his voice, and inflicted very many punishments on him, so that, afflicted at least by pain, he might stop announcing terrible things full of portents. But he, terrified neither by any fear nor by blows or heavier threats, did not change his habit or his voice, but in the same persistence of announcement, in the same sequence of words, without any interruption for pleading, he went on wailing, heedless of injury, unmoved in feeling. Thinking that this was by no means casual, but uttered in an ecstasy of mind, as indeed it was, they brought him to the judge of the place, who at that time conducted public business in that place on behalf of the Romans. He, to search out the truth, lacerated him with the most savage punishments. The more he persisted, the more violently he ordered the man to be scourged, so that if he had learned any more secret signs of the coming tumult, he might reveal them. But he neither wept nor begged, but at each blow lamented mournfully, not his own destruction, but that of his country, saying: Woe to Jerusalem. Nor, when asked who he was, or from where, or why he said these things, did he give an answer: but only pursued that lament for his country with pitiful complaint. So Albinus (for that was the man's name), wearied, released him as one in demented frenzy, not understanding what he said. But he neither held conversation with anyone, nor was heard to say anything else for the rest of the time; but singing this as a mournful and funereal song, he resounded continually by day and night: Woe to Jerusalem. He neither reviled the one who beat him, nor thanked the one who gave him food: one and the same reply, full of funereal wailing, was his to all, and especially at the celebrations of sacrifices. So for seven years and five months there was the same series of words, the same sound of voice. Thus he remained unwearied for so long a time: when the siege began, he stopped shouting those same things, as though the announcement ought to cease when the things announced were present. But when flame began to engulf the city and the temple together, going around the wall he began to cry again: Woe to the city and the people and the temple. And at the last he added: Woe also to me; and struck by a sling-stone, in the very same cry he breathed out his spirit.
CHAPTER XVII.

It was also written in ancient writings that the city with the temple would perish then, when the temple had been made square and fallen. And so, whether forgetful or stunned by the pressure of the evils bearing down on them, when the Antonia was taken they made the circuit of the temple square. Among these things the most outstanding was that which remained recorded in equally ancient writings (which they called sacred): that about that time there would be a man who would rise from their region to take rule over the whole world. This drove them into such frenzy that they promised themselves not only liberty but even kingship. Some thought this should be referred to Vespasian; the more prudent, to the Lord Jesus, who, born of Mary according to the flesh, spread his kingdom through the whole world. So, though such great signs persisted, they could not guard against what was divinely decreed. For recognising the manifest wrath of God against them, they refused to reach any remedy of consolation: so great a clouding of crime had covered the eyes of their minds.
CHAPTER XVIII.

Indeed, when their affairs too were past hope, the author of the disturbances, Eleazar, among other words of despair, lamented his rejection by God in this way: O wretched men, for what hope of this life are we keeping ourselves? Suppose the enemy pardons us: what good will it do, when God's displeasure is plain? The fires the enemy turned against us, the blasts of the winds changed, the flames turned back, so that our defences were lost. Who can live when God is against him? There is no room for pardon, but a plain command to die willingly. For why did night intervene, except that the enemy should not get ahead of us, nor break in at once with the wall's defence burnt down, but that time should be kept for us to carry out each other's deaths, and that we might die with our children and kin, so as not to see gasping old men and old women dragged off by the Romans, and our dearest wives carried off to the victor's lust? Let us die together with our fatherland, so that we do not survive in the reproach of so great a disgrace. Where then shall we flee from the face of God, or where shall we go when the Lord of heaven is hostile to us? If the mountains fall upon us and hide us in hollow caves, how shall we even so be able to escape the indignation of so great a power? For where shall we go, that God is not there, since he himself is everywhere? Or are the examples slight by which we are taught that he who formerly protected our nation has long since been hostile to it for our sins? Who could doubt this, when he sees that our hands have been turned against ourselves, and that strife at home has destroyed more than the war?
CHAPTER XIX.

I will not grant the Romans that they have conquered, nor do they claim this for themselves, who know that almost all of us have perished by our own arms rather than by foreign ones; and the Jews living at Caesarea saw [no] Roman arms, when, on the holiday of the sabbath, during the solemn worship of our rites, the multitude of the gentiles of Caesarea, inflamed by a sudden assault and a frenzy sent from above, destroyed twenty thousand of them and put all [the rest] to flight, so as to empty the whole city. Did not madness fill all Syria, so that Jews and gentiles settled in the same cities, formerly bound to one another by sharing a home, afterwards clashed with each other in arms, by which a footing for their coming victory was laid for the Romans? For what shall I say of Scythopolis? There the Jews had at first striven to forestall the gentile people, lest it plot anything against our people after the example of the other cities. And so those who ought to have fought out the war with joined strength against foreigners, these Jews on the contrary fought against one another, so that a part of them battled against their own kin and neighbours. Then they themselves, as the reward for their labour and the blood they had spent, were slain by the gentiles, [the very thing] they themselves had prevented among the gentiles. The people of Damascus, with no cause existing, laid low eight thousand Jews; the people of Ascalon, two thousand five hundred. In the city named Ptolemais also two thousand were slain. At Alexandria there was an old hatred between the Jews and the gentile peoples, from the time when Alexander the Great made use of the Jews' zeal to subdue the Egyptians: so when the city was founded, privileges were granted equally to Jews and Egyptians, and separate dwellings, so that the worship of those who wished to keep their purifications without any contamination should not be mixed. From this there were frequent clashes between them; quarrels arose, judgement was sought. Yet it is clear that nothing of so great a king's benefits was violated; but later, when a tumult was raised by the gentiles, and some of the Jews were killed and others taken off to punishment, [it is said that] the Jewish people, stirred by the wrong, rose against the authors of the wrong; and when they wished too stubbornly to take vengeance on their fellow citizens, a Roman army was brought in which slaughtered sixty thousand Jews within the city.
CHAPTER XX.

But why do I linger over lesser things, when we must lament the destruction of the whole world in the ruin of one city? Where is Jerusalem, the greatest city? Where is lovely Zion? Where is the wondrous temple? Where is that second tabernacle, the sanctuary of holiness, which once a year the chief of the priests alone used to enter, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sin of the people? It has been profaned by the gentiles: those who destroyed the city live in its remains. Where, I say, are you, city full of peoples, revered by kings, acceptable to God, seat of grace? Your pavements were of marble, your walls gleamed with marble, your roofs shone with precious marble; your gates glittered with gold, others shone with silver. All are killed, both those who dwelt in you continually and those who gathered to you from all parts of the whole world, so that there is no doubt that the whole world perished in you. All is stripped bare, burnt from the rooftops, torn down from the foundations: your dwelling has been made desolate, and there is no one to dwell in your tents; and does anyone still wish to live, and not regret having lived? Hard are the eyes that can look on these things; pitiless the minds that can wish to survive such sorrows, not because the slaughter has ceased, but because there is now no rest. For where shall we turn our eyes, or what would it please us to look upon? The whole city is a tomb of the dead: ashes meet those who look at the sun; the streets are empty of the living, full of corpses. Wretched old men, their white hair covered in ashes and their garments torn, sit upon the remains of the dead, covering the bare bones to defend them from birds and beasts. A few women are unharmed, whom an impious soldiery has kept for shame, not for life. Who, seeing these things and thinking of putting off death, would dare to lift his eyes to heaven? Who is so forgetful of his fatherland, such an enemy of his own, so estranged from piety, so devoid of sweetness, whose spirit is so soft, as of a half-man? Who is so fearful that he is not ashamed to have been kept for these things? Would that we had perished long ago, or, if life remained, that the light of our eyes had perished before we beheld the holy city torn down by the hands of enemies, and this temple, consecrated to God by our ancestors, so impiously burnt by flames, or saw the priests lying slain in the temple!
CHAPTER XXI.

Let us therefore make amends for having outlived these evils, so that we may seem to have put off death not from love of life but from the pursuit of virtue. The enemy has walled round every fortification. Nothing remains except ourselves or our wives: already they are setting our children up for auction among themselves, and contending with one another over who shall carry off whose wife, whether they are to be distributed by merit of rank or by order of persons, or whether the wretched women are to be forced to submit by lot. For us too monstrous punishments are being prepared, the most refined tortures: not only burning flames, or various deaths by the stroke of the victor's axe, a punishment harsh indeed after chains, after prison, after the yoke, but more bearable for men if it is free of mockery; but also limbs torn from the living, and above all hands cut off. And not undeservedly, since they failed in their duty when they could have helped themselves. We must also undergo the bites of wild beasts as a spectacle for the victors, which is already being celebrated in the various arenas of the cities: it ought either to shame us as an example, or to be a wondrous sight, that we should be kept to fight either with beasts or with our brothers.
CHAPTER XXII.

And many other things of this kind Eleazar set forth, full of distrust and despair. From all of which, and from the very outcome of events, when the Jews had plainly recognised that God was angry with them, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened (Rom. 1:21); and him who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24) they hated, and hating him they crucified him, and they strove to make void the glory of his resurrection. For if they had not known, they would by no means have been so guilty. Hence the Lord himself says of them: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father (John 15:22-24). They knew indeed in part, as the demons also did, saying: We know that you are the Son of God (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34): seeing marvels, hearing greater marvels; but they did not know the truth of the matter, because, hard of heart, they refused to believe. For if they had truly known by believing, they would never, as Paul says, have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). Hence the Prophet: The ox has known its owner, and the ass its master's manger; but Israel has not known me (Isa. 1:3). What is understood by the ox but every holy preacher, labouring in the seed of the word of God? What is signified by the ass but the dull people of the gentiles? Which, hearing the preaching of any shepherd, soon ran to the Lord's manger, to cling to the fodder of the word of God.
CHAPTER XXIII.

Fittingly, then, after forty-two years from his visitation Israel is banished from the land of promise, because after forty years from the departure from Egypt it is said to have been led into it; during which it received a second time the two stone tablets of the Decalogue, by which are prefigured the two years appointed to [complete] the number of the overthrow; during which also the lifting up of the bronze serpent is especially to be noted, by looking at which anyone who was dying was restored to life. For just as in that space of time they were both fed with manna, and through the mediator Moses received the law written on tablets of stone, and those who at the point of death did not look at the serpent lifted up perished: so within this time before the overthrow, refusing to partake for their salvation of the true manna (of which it had been said (John 6:51): I am the living bread that came down from heaven, etc.), and the true mediator Christ Jesus, of whom it was foretold: The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as myself, and whoever does not hear him shall be banished from his people (Deut. 18:15-18); and neglecting to follow his ordinances written in himself, the true rock; refusing, at the point of the most wretched overthrow, to believe that he was lifted up on the cross and rose from the dead, they were banished from the land of promise and perished: so that the people that sat in darkness and dwelt in the region of the shadow of death (Isa. 9:2), seeing the eternal light of the resurrection, may enter into it with its fullness; and so the remnant of Israel may be saved (Rom. 9:27), so that from two walls one Church may be joined together in the resurrection upon that cornerstone who will make both one (Eph. 2:14), our Lord Christ Jesus, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
